propositions.text: The appellant appeals the Federal Court decision dismissing her judicial review application of the Commission's vexatious complaint decision.
propositions.quote: The appellant, Tania Zulkoskey, appeals from the October 29, 2015 decision of the Federal Court (2015 FC 1196) in which the application judge dismissed her application for judicial review of the Canadian Human Rights Commission (the Commission)’s decision to not deal with her human rights complaint because it was vexatious within the meaning of paragraph 41(1)(d) of the Canadian Human Rights Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6 (the CHRA).

paragraphs.summary: The appellant appeals the Federal Court's dismissal of her judicial review of the Commission's vexatious complaint decision, says the court.

propositions.text: The appellant and spouse paid EI premiums; appellant's request for parental benefits was denied as spouse already received maximum benefits per pregnancy.
propositions.quote: The appellant and her spouse have paid Employment Insurance (EI) premiums for many years. The appellant gave birth to twins on July 10, 2009. Due to the work required to care for the twins, the appellant and her spouse each requested 35 weeks of EI parental benefits. The spouse’s request was approved. The EI Commission denied the appellant’s request on the basis that the appellant’s spouse had already received the maximum parental benefits under the Employment Insurance Act, S.C. 1996, c. 23 (the EI Act). The EI Act allows for one set of parental benefits per pregnancy.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant and spouse paid EI premiums; appellant's parental benefits request denied as spouse already received maximum benefits per pregnancy, court states.

propositions.text: The appellant appealed EI Commission's decision; appeal stayed pending Martin case outcome; stay granted without conditions.
propositions.quote: The appellant appealed the EI Commission’s decision to the Board of Referees and then to the Umpire. The issue on appeal was whether the appellant was entitled to EI parental benefits. On consent, the appellant’s appeal to the Umpire was stayed pending the outcome in Martin v. Canada (Attorney General), 2013 FCA 15, [2014] 3 F.C.R. 117 [Martin] , where a father of twins had appealed the denial of his request for a second set of EI parental benefits, additional to those received by his spouse. The appellant had initially proposed that the outcome in Martin be binding on her appeal but, ultimately, the stay was granted without conditions.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant appealed the EI decision; appeal stayed pending Martin case outcome; stay granted without conditions, court explains.

propositions.text: Martin found EI Act provides 35 weeks parental benefits per pregnancy, not per child, and scheme is not discriminatory under Charter s.15(1).
propositions.quote: In Martin, this Court found that the EI Act provides 35 weeks of parental benefits per single pregnancy or adoption, not 35 weeks per child. This Court also found that the EI parental benefits scheme is not discriminatory on the basis of family/parental status and, therefore, does not violate subsection 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (the Charter).

propositions.text: Supreme Court denied leave to appeal Martin on June 27, 2013.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court of Canada denied leave to appeal Martin on June 27, 2013 (Martin v. Canada (Attorney General), [2013] S.C.C.A. No. 122).

paragraphs.summary: Martin found EI Act provides 35 weeks per pregnancy, not per child, and is not discriminatory; Supreme Court denied leave to appeal, court reports.

propositions.text: Appeals stayed pending Martin were transferred to SST-AD, which dismissed all appeals including appellant's; appellant did not seek judicial review.
propositions.quote: All of the appeals before the Umpire that were stayed pending the outcome in Martin were transferred to the Social Security Tribunal, Appeal Division (SST-AD). The SST-AD subsequently dismissed all of the appeals, including the appellant’s appeal. The SST-AD stated that Martin settled all aspects of the issue of parental benefits and multiple-child pregnancies, including the constitutional challenge to the EI Act (AB, Tab 6(g), pp. 283-84, paras.7-8). The appellant did not seek judicial review of the SST-AD’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: Appeals stayed pending Martin were transferred to SST-AD, which dismissed all appeals including appellant's; no judicial review sought, court states.

propositions.text: Appellant filed complaint alleging 'per pregnancy' restriction discriminated on family status ground.
propositions.quote: The appellant filed a complaint with the Commission, alleging that the “per pregnancy” restriction under the EI parental benefits scheme discriminated against her on the ground of family status.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant filed complaint alleging 'per pregnancy' restriction discriminated on family status ground, court notes.

propositions.text: Commission requested appellant's position on whether complaint should not be dealt with as vexatious under CHRA s.41(1)(d).
propositions.quote: The Commission requested that the appellant provide a position letter on whether the Commission should not deal with her complaint, pursuant to paragraph 41(1)(d) of the CHRA. The Commission stated that “the issue is whether or not [the appellant’s] complaint may be vexatious” because the human rights allegations “may have already been dealt with through another process” (AB, Tab 5(a), pp. 46-49).

paragraphs.summary: Commission requested appellant's position on whether complaint should not be dealt with as vexatious under CHRA s.41(1)(d), court reports.

propositions.text: Section 40/41 Report prepared addressing vexatiousness, summarizing parties' positions, Martin case, legal tests, recommending complaint not dealt with.
propositions.quote: A Section 40/41 Report was prepared to address whether the appellant’s complaint was vexatious within the meaning of paragraph 41(1)(d) and to make a recommendation to the Commission on this basis (AB, Tab 6(l), pp. 296-298, 304, paras. 4, 8-16, 66). The Report identified the factors relating to vexatiousness, summarized the parties’ position letters, summarized the Martin case, and compared the legal tests under the CHRA and the Charter. The Report recommended that the Commission not deal with the appellant’s complaint because the appellant’s other process had “addressed the allegations of discrimination overall” (AB, Tab 6(l), p. 309, para. 98). Each party responded to the Report and availed themselves of the opportunity to respond to each other’s submissions to the Report.

paragraphs.summary: Section 40/41 Report addressed vexatiousness, summarized parties' positions and Martin, recommended complaint not dealt with, court states.

propositions.text: Commission decided not to deal with complaint adopting Section 40/41 Report's conclusion, noting SST-AD relied on Martin and allegations were essentially same.
propositions.quote: The Commission ultimately decided not to deal with the appellant’s complaint, pursuant to paragraph 41(1)(d) of the CHRA. The Commission adopted the Section 40/41 Report’s conclusion. The Commission accepted that the SST-AD relied on Martin in dismissing the appellant’s EI Act appeal and that the appellant’s allegations of discrimination were essentially the same as those decided upon by this Court in Martin, even though Martin alleged discrimination under section 15 of the Charter (AB, Tab 4, pp. 38-39).

paragraphs.summary: Commission decided not to deal with complaint adopting Section 40/41 Report's conclusion, noting SST-AD relied on Martin and allegations were same, court reports.

propositions.text: Appellant sought judicial review alleging Commission's decision was unreasonable and breached procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: The appellant sought judicial review of the Commission’s decision to not deal with her human rights complaint on the grounds that the decision was unreasonable and that the Commission breached procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant sought judicial review alleging Commission's decision was unreasonable and breached procedural fairness, court states.

propositions.text: Application judge reviewed Commission's decision on reasonableness standard, affording high deference due to discretion and policy considerations.
propositions.quote: The application judge reviewed the Commission’s decision to not deal with the appellant’s complaint on a reasonableness standard. The application judge determined that the Commission was entitled to “higher deference” and should be afforded “great latitude” because it was making a discretionary decision based on factual and policy considerations (reasons at paras. 26-27).

propositions.text: Application judge found Section 40/41 Report erred in concluding SST-AD finally determined discrimination allegations; appellant raised human rights issues only in CHRA complaint.
propositions.quote: The application judge found that the Section 40-41 Report erroneously concluded that the SST-AD finally determined the appellant’s allegations of discrimination. He found that the appellant did not raise human rights issues until she filed her CHRA complaint and that the SST-AD proceedings only dealt with the interpretation of the relevant provisions in the EI Act (reasons at para. 56).

propositions.text: Application judge concluded Commission's reliance on Martin justified decision not to deal with complaint as it negated prospect of success.
propositions.quote: The application judge concluded, however, that the Commission’s reliance on Martin, alone, justified its decision not to deal with the appellant’s complaint. The application judge stated that even though Martin involved a different complainant, the decision determined the appellant’s underlying facts and arguments such that it “negates any prospect for success in her case” (reasons at para. 65).

paragraphs.summary: Application judge reviewed Commission's decision as reasonable with high deference, found report erred on SST-AD's role, but reliance on Martin justified dismissal, court reports.

propositions.text: Application judge held procedural fairness standard is correctness; appellant owed lesser degree of fairness per Baker factors.
propositions.quote: The application judge determined that the standard of review for determining procedural fairness is correctness. Based on the Baker factors, the appellant was owed a lesser degree of procedural fairness (reasons at para. 42).

propositions.text: Application judge found Commission informed appellant of considerations, gave ample opportunity to submit, and report was neutral, thorough, and accurate.
propositions.quote: The application judge found that the Commission informed the appellant of what it would consider in deciding whether to deal with her complaint and gave her ample opportunity to provide submissions. The application judge found that the Section 40/41 Report, upon which the Commission based its decision, was neutral and sufficiently thorough, accurately summarized the parties’ submissions, and comprehensively examined the factors to determine whether a claim is vexatious (reasons at paras. 43-45).

paragraphs.summary: Application judge held procedural fairness standard is correctness; found Commission gave fair process and report was thorough and neutral, court states.

propositions.text: Issues on appeal: correct standard of review, reasonableness of Commission's decision, procedural fairness of decision.
propositions.quote: I would characterize the issues on appeal as follows: 1. What is the correct standard of review to be applied to the Commission’s decision to not deal with the appellant’s complaint? 2. Was the Commission’s decision to not deal with the appellant’s complaint reasonable? 3. Was the Commission’s decision to not deal with the appellant’s complaint procedurally fair?

paragraphs.summary: Court states issues on appeal: standard of review, reasonableness, and procedural fairness of Commission's decision.

propositions.text: On judicial review appeal, court must determine if application judge chose and applied correct standard of review, stepping into their shoes.
propositions.quote: On an appeal of an application for judicial review, this Court must determine whether the application judge chose the correct standard of review and applied it properly. In doing so, this Court “step[s] into the shoes” of the Federal Court judge (Agraira v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36 at paras. 45-47, [2013] 2 S.C.R. 559).

paragraphs.summary: Court states it must determine if application judge chose and applied correct standard of review, stepping into their shoes.

propositions.text: Parties agreed on reasonableness standard; court finds this appropriate and focuses on whether decision was reasonable under vexatious ground.
propositions.quote: The parties agreed that the Commission’s decision not to deal with the appellant’s complaint is to be reviewed on a reasonableness standard. While their agreement does not bind me, I find that the parties have settled on the appropriate standard of review (Bergeron v. Canada (Attorney General), 2015 FCA 160 at para. 40, 255 A.C.W.S. (3d) 955 [Bergeron]). The parties spent considerable effort in making arguments that would either decrease, on the part of the appellant, or increase on the part of the respondent, the “margin of appreciation” to be afforded the Commission in reaching its decision. In my view, analyzing reasonableness in an attempt to assign some greater or lesser amount of deference to the Commission is of no assistance here. In this matter, the question to be answered is, given the overall context, was the Commission’s decision not to deal with the appellant’s complaint based upon the vexatious ground set out in paragraph 41(1)(d) reasonable. Nothing more and nothing less (see Wilson v. Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd., 2016 SCC 29 at paras. 18, 73, 399 D.L.R (4th) 193).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds parties' agreement on reasonableness standard appropriate and focuses on whether decision was reasonable under vexatious ground.

propositions.text: Section 40/41 Report is part of Commission's reasons; Commission's decision copies report's conclusion verbatim.
propositions.quote: This Court should consider the Section 40/41 Report as part of the Commission’s reasons for its decision to not deal with the appellant’s complaint (Sketchley v. Canada (Attorney General), 2005 FCA 404 at para. 37, [2006] 3 F.C.R. 392; Bergeron at para. 60). The Commission’s decision consists of a verbatim copy of the conclusion contained in the Section 40/41 Report.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Section 40/41 Report is part of Commission's reasons; decision copies report's conclusion verbatim.

propositions.text: Commission informed appellant it considered complaint vexatious if issues already dealt with in another process.
propositions.quote: The Commission informed the appellant that it was considering whether or not to deal with her complaint as it may be “vexatious” under paragraph 41(1)(d). The Commission considers a complaint vexatious where “the human rights issues in [the] complaint may have already been dealt with through another process” (AB, Tab 5(a), pp. 46-49; Tab 6(l), p. 296, p. 304, paras. 4, 9, 66).

paragraphs.summary: Court states Commission informed appellant it considered complaint vexatious if issues already dealt with in another process.

propositions.text: Figliola case interprets similar provision as reflecting finality doctrines: issue estoppel, collateral attack, abuse of process.
propositions.quote: In British Columbia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Figliola, 2011 SCC 52, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 422 [Figliola], the Supreme Court considered a provision of the British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, para. 27(1)(f), that is similar to paragraph 41(1)(d) in the CHRA. A complaint could be dismissed where “the substance of the complaint or that part of the complaint has been appropriately dealt with in another proceeding”. Justice Abella found that the provision reflected the principles of the doctrines of finality – issue estoppel, collateral attack and abuse of process (Figliola at paras. 24-25).

propositions.text: Bergeron summarized Figliola factors: concurrent jurisdiction, same legal issue, opportunity to know and meet case.
propositions.quote: In Bergeron, this Court summarized the Figliola factors used to assess whether a human rights complaint has already been dealt with in a prior proceeding (at para. 50): Was there concurrent jurisdiction to decide human rights issues? Was the legal issue in the alternate forum essentially the same as the legal issue in the human rights complaint? Did the complainant have the opportunity to know the case to meet and have a chance to meet it? Figliola and Bergeron addressed circumstances where the same complainant received a final decision on allegations of discrimination in a prior proceeding then raised discrimination again in a human rights proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains Figliola and Bergeron cases interpret similar provision reflecting finality doctrines and set factors for vexatiousness.

propositions.text: Commission's approach to vexatiousness reflects Figliola factors, considering final decision, authority, issue similarity, opportunity to raise issues, and process differences.
propositions.quote: The Commission’s stated approach to vexatiousness reflects the Figliola factors. As shown in the Commission’s correspondence with the appellant and the Section 40/41 Report, the Commission considers the following factors when deciding whether or not a complaint is vexatious (AB, Tab 5(a), pp. 48-49; Tab 65(l), pp. 297-98, para. 16): Has a final decision been made in another process? Did the decision-maker in the other process have the authority to decide human rights issues? Were the issues raised during the other process essentially the same as the issues in this complaint? Were all the human rights issues addressed? Did the complainant have a chance to raise all relevant human rights issues? Is there a significant difference between the other process and the Commission process?

paragraphs.summary: Court states Commission's vexatiousness approach reflects Figliola factors considering final decision, authority, issue similarity, opportunity, and process differences.

propositions.text: Section 40/41 Report identifies appellant's other process as SST-AD EI appeal relying on Martin; both had jurisdiction; allegations essentially same; Martin's Charter analysis suffices for CHRA.
propositions.quote: The Section 40/41 Report identifies the appellant’s other process as her EI Act appeal before the SST-AD (AB, Tab 6(l), pp. 304, 309, paras. 67, 96). The Report emphasizes that the SST-AD relied on this Court’s decision in Martin to dismiss the appellant’s appeal (AB, Tab 6(l), pp. 304-309, paras. 67, 73, 75, 96). The Commission’s reasons state that both the SST-AD and this Court had jurisdiction to decide human rights issues (AB, Tab 6(l), pp. 305, 309, paras. 71, 96). The reasons also state that the allegations of discrimination in the appellant’s CHRA complaint are essentially the same as those raised and finally decided on by the SST-AD in the appellant’s EI Act appeal and by this Court in Martin under section 15 of the Charter (AB, Tab 6(l), pp. 305-306, 308, paras. 75-77, 96). The investigator acknowledges that the appellant did not raise the CHRA before the SST-AD. However, the Commission concludes that Martin’s Charter analysis, on which the SST-AD relied, sufficiently examined the appellant’s allegations of discrimination and would be similar to an analysis under the CHRA (AB, Tab 6(l), pp. 305, 308-309, paras. 76, 92, 96-97).

paragraphs.summary: Court states Section 40/41 Report identifies appellant's other process as SST-AD EI appeal relying on Martin; both had jurisdiction; allegations same; Martin's Charter analysis suffices for CHRA.

propositions.text: The Commission unreasonably applied paragraph 41(1)(d) to the appellant's complaint.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Commission unreasonably applied paragraph 41(1)(d) to the appellant’s complaint.

propositions.text: The appellant did not raise human rights issues before filing her CHRA complaint; SST-AD's decision was limited to statutory interpretation under EI Act.
propositions.quote: Counsel for the respondent conceded that the appellant did not raise human rights issues prior to filing her CHRA complaint and that the SST-AD’s decision was limited to the statutory interpretation of the relevant EI Act provisions.

propositions.text: SST-AD applied Martin to find appellant entitled to one set of benefits per pregnancy, not per child, under EI Act.
propositions.quote: The SST-AD only applied Martin to find that, under the EI Act, the appellant was entitled to a single set of benefits per pregnancy, not per child.

propositions.text: Appellant did not raise discrimination allegations under Charter or CHRA to which SST-AD could apply Martin.
propositions.quote: The appellant did not raise any allegations of discrimination, under the Charter or the CHRA, to which the SST-AD could have applied Martin.

propositions.text: Appellant did not receive a final decision on human rights issues at SST-AD.
propositions.quote: The appellant did not receive a final decision regarding human rights issues at the SST-AD.

propositions.text: Vexatiousness and Figliola factors do not apply as appellant is not re-litigating a final decision issue.
propositions.quote: As the appellant is not attempting to re-litigate an issue on which she has already received a final decision, vexatiousness and the Figliola factors do not apply to the appellant’s CHRA complaint.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Commission unreasonably applied paragraph 41(1)(d); respondent concedes no prior human rights issues raised; SST-AD limited to EI Act interpretation; appellant did not raise discrimination or receive final human rights decision; vexatiousness does not apply.

propositions.text: Commission could reasonably dismiss complaint based on Martin alone if complaint has no reasonable prospect of success.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues that the Commission could reasonably dismiss the appellant’s complaint based on Martin alone.

propositions.text: A complaint with no reasonable prospect of success is frivolous under paragraph 41(1)(d).
propositions.quote: However, such a complaint would be considered frivolous within the meaning of paragraph 41(1)(d) (Love v. Canada(Privacy Commissioner), 2015 FCA 198 at para. 23, 259 A.C.W.S. (3d) 130).

propositions.text: Commission limited its analysis to vexatiousness and appellant's process, not frivolousness or discrimination evidence.
propositions.quote: Although frivolous is included alongside vexatious in paragraph 41(1)(d), the Commission clearly limited its analysis to the factors relating to vexatiousness and the appellant’s other process.

propositions.text: Commission asked parties to provide submissions on vexatiousness only, excluding discrimination evidence.
propositions.quote: The Commission asked the parties to provide submissions on vexatiousness only and to not include evidence related to the allegations of discrimination (AB, Tab 5(a), pp. 47-49; Tab 5(c), p. 150).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues dismissal based on Martin if no success prospect; court notes frivolous means no prospect; Commission limited analysis to vexatiousness and excluded discrimination evidence submissions.

propositions.text: Vexatious ground in paragraph 41(1)(d) is interpreted flexibly to prevent multiple proceedings and resource waste.
propositions.quote: I recognize that the vexatious ground in paragraph 41(1)(d) is intended to be interpreted flexibly to prevent multiplicity of proceedings and waste of resources on re-litigation (Figliola at para. 36).

propositions.text: This Court adjudicated Mr. Martin’s Charter discrimination allegations.
propositions.quote: This Court adjudicated Mr. Martin’s allegations of discrimination under the Charter.

propositions.text: Martin's discrimination allegations may be essentially the same as appellant’s CHRA complaint, so complaint may fail.
propositions.quote: The allegations of discrimination in Martin may be essentially the same as those raised in the appellant’s CHRA complaint. On this basis, the appellant’s complaint may inevitably fail.

propositions.text: Commission based decision solely on vexatiousness requiring final decision on discrimination allegations, which appellant lacks.
propositions.quote: However, the Commission based its decision to not deal with the appellant’s complaint solely on vexatiousness which raises particular legal principles, specifically that the appellant must have received a final decision on her allegations of discrimination.

propositions.text: Martin’s adjudication cannot substitute for appellant’s final decision on discrimination allegations.
propositions.quote: The adjudication of Mr. Martin’s allegations of discrimination cannot be used as a substitute.

propositions.text: Commission’s decision is not within acceptable outcomes under vexatious ground in paragraph 41(1)(d).
propositions.quote: As a result, the Commission’s decision does not fall within a range of acceptable and defensible outcomes that could be reached under the ground of vexatious in paragraph 41(1)(d).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains vexatiousness prevents re-litigation; Martin's discrimination adjudicated; appellant's complaint may fail but lacks final decision; Commission wrongly relied solely on vexatiousness; decision not acceptable.

propositions.text: Commission misunderstood SST-AD’s dismissal basis, leading to vexatiousness inquiry.
propositions.quote: The Commission misconceived the basis of the SST-AD’s dismissal of the appellant’s appeal from the decision of the EI Commission. This led the Commission to ask itself whether the appellant’s CHRA complaint was vexatious.

propositions.text: If Commission properly understood SST-AD and Martin, it could raise frivolousness with appellant and decide complaint's prospect of success.
propositions.quote: Had the Commission properly understood the basis of the SST-AD’s dismissal and, had it thought that this Court’s decision in Martin was conclusive on the issue raised in the appellant’s complaint, it could have properly raised this with the appellant. After hearing the appellant’s submissions on this point, the Commission could have decided whether the complaint was frivolous, in the narrow legal sense of having no prospect of success.

propositions.text: Commission may reconsider complaint and not proceed if it has no prospect of success to manage scarce resources.
propositions.quote: In my view, this approach is still open to the Commission when it reconsiders the matter. The Commission must manage scarce resources; it is open to the Commission to not proceed with a complaint that, in its view, has no prospect of success.

propositions.text: Court does not believe appellant’s complaint is frivolous in colloquial sense and recognizes its importance.
propositions.quote: I wish to make it clear that I do not believe that the appellant’s complaint is frivolous in the colloquial sense of the term. I appreciate that this matter is very important to the appellant and to those in similar circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Commission misunderstood SST-AD dismissal, should have considered frivolousness with appellant; Commission may reconsider complaint; court values complaint's importance.

propositions.text: No need to decide procedural fairness breach; appellant's submissions on this are without merit.
propositions.quote: Given my conclusion above, it is not necessary to determine whether the Commission breached procedural fairness in coming to its decision to not deal with the appellant’s complaint. However, in my view, the appellant’s submissions on this issue are without merit.

propositions.text: Commission did not promise to consider appellant’s original position letter unambiguously.
propositions.quote: The Commission did not make a clear, unambiguous, and unqualified promise that it would consider the appellant’s original position letter when making its decision on whether to deal with her complaint.

propositions.text: Initial correspondence stated Commission would use parties’ submissions to the report.
propositions.quote: The initial correspondence to the appellant stated that the Commission would use “the parties’ submissions to the report” (AB, Tab 5(a), p. 46).

propositions.text: Correspondence seeking appellant’s submissions to Section 40/41 Report stated Commission would decide based on report, complaint form, and submissions received.
propositions.quote: Correspondence seeking the appellant’s submissions to the Section 40/41 Report stated (AB, Tab 5(c), p. 150): The Commission will decide based on the [Report], the complaint form, and any submissions (comments) it has received from the parties.

propositions.text: Commission clearly communicated it would consider submissions made in response to Section 40/41 Report and followed this procedure.
propositions.quote: The Commission clearly communicated that it would consider the parties’ submissions that were made in response to the Section 40/41 Report. The Commission followed this stated procedure in coming to its decision.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no procedural fairness breach; appellant's submissions lack merit; Commission did not promise to consider original letter; Commission communicated and followed procedure to consider submissions to report.

propositions.text: Appellant had full opportunity to present position on why Commission should deal with complaint.
propositions.quote: The appellant was provided a full opportunity to present her position on why the Commission should deal with her complaint.

propositions.text: Arguments in original position letter repeated in Section 40/41 Report, including limited SST-AD scope, inapplicability of Martin, and burden on Commission to dismiss only plain and obvious cases.
propositions.quote: The arguments made in her original position letter were repeated in the Section 40/41 Report, including: the limited scope of the SST-AD proceeding; the inapplicability of Martin; and the heavy burden on the Commission to only dismiss complaints in plain and obvious cases.

propositions.text: Commission reviewed appellant’s submissions to the Report and response to respondent’s submissions.
propositions.quote: In addition to the Section 40/41 Report, the Commission specifically reviewed the appellant’s submissions to the Report and the appellant’s response to the respondent’s submissions to the Report.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds appellant had full opportunity to present position; original arguments repeated in report; Commission reviewed appellant's submissions and responses.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed with costs; matter referred back to Commission for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal, with costs, and refer the matter back to the Commission for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows appeal with costs and refers matter back to Commission for reconsideration.
